## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.02938.026](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.02938.026)

eLife posts the editorial decision letter and author response on a selection of the published articles (subject to the approval of the authors). An edited version of the letter sent to the authors after peer review is shown, indicating the substantive concerns or comments; minor concerns are not usually shown. Reviewers have the opportunity to discuss the decision before the letter is sent (see review process). Similarly, the author response typically shows only responses to the major concerns raised by the reviewers.

Thank you for sending your work entitled “A network of sensory-motor neurons and dopaminergic support cells couples ejaculation and satiation in C. elegans males” for consideration at eLife. Your article has been favorably evaluated by Eve Marder (Senior editor) and 4 reviewers, one of whom, Peggy Mason, is a member of our Board of Reviewing Editors.

The Reviewing editor and the other reviewers discussed their comments before we reached this decision, and the Reviewing editor has assembled the following comments to help you prepare a revised submission.

This is a comprehensive look at an interesting phenomenon – the post-ejaculatory refractory period – in worms. The authors used many different methods to attack this problem. They come up with an important contribution that answers many of the first order questions while also making clear that the topic is sufficiently rich with complexity to warrant further study.

The reviewers who were unfamiliar with the worm field found reading the manuscript challenging. It was hard to follow. Remember that the length of eLife papers is not proscribed but is the length needed to convey the story, no more and no less, so please revise for clarity. Overall, the Introduction and Discussion should place the work within the context of what is known in the C. elegans literature. Definitions of refractory period and of satiation should be provided in the Introduction. Please note that the literature in mammals clearly differentiates between refractory period and satiation and there is evidence for different neural circuits controlling them. The situation may be different in worm – the authors seem to convey that the two phenomenons are identical in C. elegans.

The figures are very difficult to make out. For example, Figure 1 is very difficult to make out both in terms of color and arrangement. Parts B and C are ok but Parts A and D are not readable and should be extensively revised. I recommend an overhaul of the schematic figures. Where the point to be made is highly anatomical (e.g. which muscles support ejaculation), keep the anatomical relationships intact in the diagram. However, where the points are circuit-related, uncouple the diagrams from anatomical representation. Don't make the cells or structures or muscles anatomically sized or arranged. In other words, move away from the strict anatomy and stylize the topography with some extra space between cellular and muscle elements. Use black and white and patterns: the colors are hard to discern. And please increase the size of the figures. Space is not a particular concern but readability is.

One of the tenets upon which this work rests is that the refractory period is useful because it allows the animal to recover to ejaculate again. But unless we missed it (and this is entirely possible) the authors do not test this. The test is easy. When the refractory period is shortened, is sperm count reduced?

Relating the disorders to pathologies such as eating disorders and drug addiction is an inappropriate stretch. In mammals, satiety in food intake is a completely different event with a completely different neural regulation than mating-induced satiety. All discussion or hints of relations of the current findings in C. elegans with those in rodent literature of food intake (or addiction) are suspect, and need to be omitted or substantially toned down. This includes the first paragraph of the Introduction and last paragraph of the Discussion.

It would be worthwhile for the authors to speculate on the relationship between their results and ejaculatory control in mammals. The circuitry controlling ejaculation is well described in rodents and that literature is directly relevant to the studies here, yet not discussed or cited. In addition, there is peripheral modulation of the corpus cavernosum by dopamine and in fact other monoamines, most strikingly serotonin. There may be a general theme here of monoaminergic modulation of sexual motor acts. In comparing the findings to work in mammals, it is also noteworthy that refractory period in worms is defined strictly on the basis of re-initiation of mating. Is this independent of a neural network in the head? If so, that would make it very different from the situation in mammals, where the post ejaculatory refractory period appears to be controlled by networks in hypothalamus, amygdala, and septal nuclei. Some discussion on this would be helpful.

Could the laser ablation phenotypes have been caused by non-specific injury? This is unlikely given the consistency of these results with the rest of the story, but should be commented on.

In the last paragraphs of the Introduction and in the last paragraph of the Discussion the authors comment that the refractory period is likely to aid “recovery” and/or “resetting”. However, they do not comment on what might need to recover or what in the neuromuscular network might need resetting during the recovery period. It would be interesting to know more about their thoughts on this matter (or at least if they found this puzzling).

The refractory period was defined as including both reduced mating drive and less-efficient execution of mating. Defects in gonad-ablated and linker-cell-ablated males suggest the refractory period is subject to regulation, which is the authors' primary conclusion from these experiments. However, it is interesting that failure to transfer sperm leads to a lengthened refractory period in some animals. Why would this be the case? The authors are invited to speculate on this point in the Discussion.

The timing of Ca2+ transients in SPD, SPV, and SPC neurons and the gonadal valve suggests these neurons promote sperm transfer. Valve transients can be induced by an ACh agonist, consistent with being regulated by SPC, and show altered kinetics of decay in spicule tips-ablated males. Data from wild-type males suggest a role for SPC in initiation followed by SPD/SPV in continued movement. However, ablation of SPV/SPD slowed the increase of Ca2+ in SPC, suggesting the spicule neurons actually promote initiation of release via SPC as well as transfer. These results are apparently conflicting. Why does the SPC peak more rapidly than SPV/SPD? This point seems worth addressing, at least by discussing more fully.

ChR2 stimulation of several groups of neurons were used to evoke “artificial” ejaculation. Curiously, expression in a wide range of cells is necessary for evoked ejaculation. This assay is likely to be useful for subsequent studies in this and other labs. Here, the glutamatergic p.c.s. neuron PCA along with SPC/PCB were shown to promote ejaculation. High PCA Ca2+ transients occurred after insertion and decreased at the initiation of sperm transfer. SPV/SPD were not required for artificial ejaculation, suggesting they function upstream of the relevant ChR2-expressing cells; their ablation had no effect on Ca2+ in PCA or PCB.

Socket cells of the spicule promote sperm movement into the hermaphrodite and show a rapid increase in transients during mating like those of SPC and the valve. Dopamine synthesis is required in the socket cells rather than in ray neurons for sperm transfer. Socket cell DA also promotes the refractory period. One question that arises based on the presented model is whether exogenous dopamine is sufficient to induce a “refractory period” in the absence of prior mating.

results.result: C. elegans males exhibit a post-ejaculatory refractory period of approximately 12 minutes, during which sexual drive is temporarily suppressed. Males commence mating within 34 seconds and maintain spicule insertion for an average of 94 seconds, but require approximately 5 minutes before re-executing copulation after spicule retraction.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C8 provide converging behavioral evidence from timed observations (C2, C3, C5, C6, C7) that collectively establish the existence and duration of the refractory period (C3, C4) and temporary suppression of sexual drive (C8). The measurements are specific, include standard deviations, and are supported by Figure 3A-B.

results.result: Different components of male mating behavior recover at different rates during the refractory period, with males passing over the vulva significantly more times during the second mating bout compared to the first.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C10 demonstrate differential recovery of sensory-motor circuits through quantitative behavioral measurements (C9) supported by Figure 3D. The inference about differential circuit recovery (C10) is reasonable given the observed behavioral differences.

results.result: Males with longer refractory periods (9-30 min) sire more progeny in the second mating than males with shorter refractory periods (3-8:59 min), while both groups sire similar numbers of progeny in the first mating. This indicates that a longer refractory period allows males to recover their ability to sire progeny.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C13 provide progeny count data (C11, C12) from Figure 3E demonstrating that refractory period length correlates with reproductive success in the second mating. The control showing no difference in first mating (C12) strengthens the conclusion that recovery time matters (C13).

results.result: The gonad, specifically the germ line, sends a signal to promote mating behavior. Males lacking gonad structures or germ line require longer time to commence mating, but after spicule insertion and retraction, their refractory period resembles controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C18 use laser ablation experiments (Figures 3F-G) to demonstrate the gonad's role in promoting initial mating drive. The similarity between gonad-ablated and germ line-ablated males (C17) supports the inference that the germ line is required (C18). The refractory period data (C16) provides important controls.

results.result: Preventing sperm release by linker cell ablation increases the duration of the refractory period in some males, suggesting the refractory period is plastic and can be modified by cellular components that sense sperm release.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C20 use linker cell ablation to uncouple sperm production from release, revealing bimodal refractory period responses (Figure 3G). The observation that some males compensate while others don't (C20) is supported by the data showing two populations with different refractory periods.

results.result: The SPV and SPD sensory neurons, located in the spicules with sensory endings exposed at the tips, modify the duration of the refractory period. Cutting spicule tips in adult males results in significantly shorter refractory periods (296±217s vs 499±224s, p=0.0121) without affecting initial mating response times.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C27 establish SPV/SPD anatomy (C21-C22) and use two experimental approaches: larval ablation showing variable defects (C23) and adult spicule tip cutting showing specific refractory period effects (C24-C26, Figure 3G). The statistical comparison (C26) with appropriate controls (C25) supports the conclusion (C27).

results.result: Spicule tips-cut males show impaired ejaculation: the valve opens in only half of operated males (8/15 vs 12/13 controls, p=0.0377), sperm rarely passes into the hermaphrodite (1/15 vs 10/14 controls, p=0.0005), and no operated males sired progeny at first mating compared to 67% of controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C32 provide multiple lines of evidence (valve opening, sperm transfer, progeny counts) from Figures 4A-B with statistical tests showing that spicule sensilla promote both sperm movement and affect the refractory period (C32). The convergent defects support the conclusion.

results.result: During the second mating, spicule tips-cut males inserted and retracted their spicules multiple times with each penetration lasting only a few seconds, indicating defects in entering or maintaining the ejaculatory state.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C34 describe a specific behavioral phenotype (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2) that differs from wild-type sustained insertion. The inference about ejaculatory state defects (C34) is reasonable given the abnormal insertion pattern.

results.result: Calcium imaging reveals coordinated activity in SPV/SPD and SPC neurons during mating. SPV/SPD Ca2+ transients peak at ~4s post-intromission and decline during sperm movement. SPC Ca2+ transients increase more rapidly (peak at 1.3s vs 4.0s, p<0.05) and also decline during sperm movement.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C39 present calcium imaging data (Figures 5A-B, Table 1) with specific timing measurements and statistical comparisons. The temporal dynamics of both cell types are well-documented with n=5 and appropriate controls (mDsRed reference).

results.result: The acetylcholine agonist oxotremorine S (OxoS) induces males to protrude spicules and increases gonadal Ca2+ transients (n=5), indicating that somatic gonad activity can be stimulated by ACh.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C42 use pharmacological manipulation (OxoS) to demonstrate ACh responsiveness of the gonad (Figure 5C). The observation of increased Ca2+ transients (C41) supports the inference about ACh stimulation (C42), though OxoS is noted as potentially non-specific.

results.result: The gonadal valve shows rapid Ca2+ transient increases upon spicule insertion (peak at ~1.8s), remaining high until valve opening (~6.9±1.5s). In spicule-tips cut males, Ca2+ transient decrease is more gradual, the valve fails to open in 10/19 males (vs 18/19 controls, p=0.0078), and sperm transfer fails (1/19 vs 18/19 controls, p<0.0001).
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C50 combine calcium imaging (Figures 5D-F, Table 1) with behavioral outcomes, showing that SPV/SPD neurons are necessary for proper valve function. The statistical comparisons (C48, C50) and multiple measures (Ca2+ dynamics, valve opening, sperm transfer) provide strong convergent evidence.

results.result: Calcium imaging suggests that upon intromission, the SPC primes the gonad for ejaculation initiation, while spicule sensory neurons provide further stimulation necessary for sperm movement and release.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C52 synthesize calcium imaging and ablation data to propose a model of coordinated cellular function. The temporal coordination of SPC and valve activity (C51) and the requirement for SPV/SPD for complete sperm release (C52) are supported by the imaging and ablation experiments.

results.result: Optogenetic experiments show that expressing ChR2 from individual promoters (Pgar-3b, Punc-103B, Punc-17, or Punc-17S) fails to induce ejaculation, but simultaneous expression from Punc-103B, Punc-17S, and Pgar-3B promoters does induce ejaculation, indicating that multiple cell types including SPD, SPC, PCA, PCB neurons, head neurons, and sex muscles must be stimulated.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C55 use systematic optogenetic experiments (Figures 6A-C) to demonstrate that ejaculation requires coordinated activation of multiple cell types. The negative results with single promoters (C53) and positive result with combined promoters (C54) support the conclusion about circuit complexity (C55).

results.result: In ChR2-expressing males, single ablations of SPV/SPD, SPC, or PCB do not significantly reduce light-induced ejaculation (p=0.78, 0.42, 0.2 respectively), but ablating both SPC and PCB significantly reduces ejaculation (42%, p=0.013). PCA ablation dramatically reduces ejaculation (16%, p=0.0003), revealing a role for PCA in promoting ejaculation.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C61 use systematic ablation in ChR2 background (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1) with appropriate statistical tests. The pattern of results reveals redundancy (C56-C59) and identifies PCA as critical (C60-C61). Sample sizes and p-values are provided.

results.result: Sex muscles show a peak in Ca2+ transients immediately upon spicule intromission, then display a second increase ~11s later coincident with ejaculation initiation when gubernaculum and anal depressor muscles become hyper-contracted. Sperm is detected in the hermaphrodite uterus after ~15-20s, followed by oscillating Ca2+ transients in muscles.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C65 describe the temporal dynamics of muscle activity during mating using calcium imaging (Table 1, Figures 7A-B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1). The biphasic response and oscillations are clearly documented with specific timing measurements.

results.result: PCA Ca2+ transients gradually increase after spicule insertion with first peak at 6.3±0.56s (n=5) and remain elevated after sperm release. The timing of peak PCA activity (9.2±2.9s) precedes and overlaps with the second Ca2+ increase in gubernaculum muscles (11±3.9s, p=0.8), suggesting PCA promotes these muscle changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C69 use calcium imaging (Table 1, Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1) to establish temporal correlation between PCA activity and muscle contractions. The statistical comparison (C68) and temporal precedence support the inference that PCA promotes muscle changes (C69).

results.result: Laser-ablation of PCA does not have gross effects on vulva location, spicule intromission, or ejaculation, likely because PCB and PCC neurons can compensate for the damaged PCA cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C71 reconcile the lack of phenotype in PCA ablation during normal mating with the strong optogenetic phenotype. The compensation hypothesis (C71) is supported by connectome data showing similar connections and previous studies (Liu and Sternberg, 1995; Liu et al., 2011).

results.result: Removing SPV/SPD neurons does not affect PCA or dorsal sex muscle activity, indicating these are not downstream of SPV/SPD. However, SPC Ca2+ transients increase at a slower rate when SPV/SPD are removed, suggesting SPV/SPD promote SPC activity upon insertion.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C75 use calcium imaging in spicule-tips cut males (Figures 8A-D, supplements) to map circuit relationships. The differential effects on PCA/muscles (C72) vs SPC (C74) with appropriate controls (Table 1) support the circuit organization conclusions (C73, C75).

results.result: PCB Ca2+ transients show minor increases upon insertion that quickly dissipate, and this activity is unaffected by SPV/SPD removal. This suggests PCB does not play a significant role after insertion but can compensate for SPC loss in promoting light-induced ejaculation.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C79 use calcium imaging (Figure 8E, Figure 8—figure supplement 4) to characterize PCB activity. The minimal and transient response (C76-C77) supports the inference about limited post-insertion role (C78). The compensation hypothesis (C79) reconciles optogenetic and imaging data.

results.result: Laser-ablation of all eight spicule socket cell nuclei in adult males does not affect insertion (7/22 ablated vs 11/27 controls, p=0.6) but significantly impairs sperm release: only 1/7 ablated males released sperm for ≥10s compared to 8/11 (73%) controls (p=0.0498). Removing SPV/SPD with socket cells has more significant impact than socket cells alone.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C84 use adult socket cell ablation to dissect function, showing specific effects on sperm release (C81-C82) without affecting insertion (C80). Statistical tests support the conclusion that socket cells promote sperm release (C83). Comparison to spicule tip cutting (C84) reveals additive effects.

results.result: Socket cell Ca2+ transients increase rapidly upon insertion with a profile similar to SPC and gonadal valve, then decline to about half peak intensity at sperm release. This supports the hypothesis that socket cells are directly involved in ejaculatory behaviors.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C87 use calcium imaging (Table 1, Figure 9A, Figure 9—figure supplement 2) to demonstrate socket cell activity during mating. The temporal dynamics (C85-C86) directly contradict the alternative hypothesis that socket cells are structurally inert, supporting direct involvement (C87).

results.result: The dopamine synthesis enzymes tyrosine hydroxylase (cat-2) and aromatic amino acid decarboxylase (bas-1) are expressed in socket cells. In contrast, DA-expressing rays R5A, R7A, and R9A show no gross changes in Ca2+ transients after spicule insertion, suggesting socket cells, not ray neurons, are the source of DA for ejaculation.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C90 combine expression data (Figure 9—figure supplement 1) with calcium imaging (Figure 9B, Figure 9—figure supplement 2) to identify the relevant DA source. The differential activity patterns between socket cells and rays (C89) support the inference about DA source (C90).

results.result: cat-2(lf) mutant males have difficulty releasing or sustaining sperm release, with only 31% successfully transferring sperm for ≥10s compared to 79% of wild-type (p=0.02). While exogenous DA reduces ectopic intromission attempts in cat-2(lf) males, it does not restore sperm transfer ability.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C94 characterize cat-2(lf) phenotypes (Figure 9C-D) showing specific ejaculation defects (C91-C92) with statistical support. The differential rescue by exogenous DA (C93-C94) suggests distinct DA sources or mechanisms for different mating behaviors.

results.result: Expressing cat-2(+) in dopaminergic rays and socket cells using Pcat-2 rescues both ectopic intromission and ejaculation defects. However, expressing cat-2 only in ray neurons using Pdat-1 rescues ectopic intromission but not sperm transfer, demonstrating that DA synthesis in socket cells is necessary for sperm release.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C97 use cell-specific rescue experiments (Figures 9C-D) to definitively identify socket cells as the critical DA source for ejaculation. The differential rescue with Pcat-2 vs Pdat-1 (C95-C96) provides strong evidence for the conclusion (C97).

results.result: Transgenic cat-2(lf) males expressing cat-2(+) in rays and socket cells or just rays commence first mating in similar timeframes (51s vs 121s, p=0.08). However, males lacking cat-2(+) in socket cells have shorter refractory periods (518s vs 1083s, p=0.0127), indicating DA contributes to refractory period length.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C100 use cell-specific rescue to dissect DA's role in the refractory period (Figure 9E). The statistical comparison (C99) with appropriate controls (C98) supports the conclusion that socket cell DA regulates refractory period duration (C100).

results.result: While 15 and 20 mM exogenous DA non-significantly slow spicule insertion, 25 mM DA significantly increases insertion time, with few males inserting within 5 min. This decreased mating ability is not due to sluggish movement or paralysis (backing velocity 171±43 vs 178±35 μm/s), demonstrating that exogenous DA can interfere with mating ability.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C105 use dose-response experiments (Figure 9F, Figure 9—figure supplement 1) with appropriate controls for general motor function (C104). The concentration-dependent effect (C101-C103) and control measurements support the conclusion about DA interference (C105).

results.result: The refractory period is dependent on males' ability to produce and sense successful ejaculation. A longer refractory period allows males to recover sperm transfer ability, while attempting to mate too quickly reduces progeny siring. This may help ensure males copulate with different partners.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C110 synthesize the functional significance of the refractory period. The relationship between refractory period length and reproductive success (C107-C108) is supported by progeny data. The hypothesis about promoting mating with different partners (C109) is reasonable speculation based on the data.

results.result: The authors propose that SPV and SPD sense the intrauterine environment, promote sperm release, and regulate the refractory period. The SPC neurons, with support from SPV/SPD and post cloacal sensilla, trigger ejaculation initiation via direct cholinergic signaling to the gonad. SPV and SPD help maintain a lower threshold in SPC, preventing premature ejaculation.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C114 present mechanistic models based on calcium imaging, ablation, and optogenetic data. While these are proposed models (C111, C113, C114), they are well-supported by the experimental evidence presented throughout the manuscript, including connectome data (Jarrell et al., 2012).

results.result: The gubernaculum muscles contract to facilitate sperm release, likely by re-adjusting spicule position. PCA (which expresses glutamate transporter eat-4) is partially responsible for promoting these contractions, with peak activity (9.2±2.9s) corresponding to muscle contractions. PCB and PCC can compensate for PCA loss. However, PCA activity and muscle contractions are insufficient for sperm release without SPV/SPD and socket cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C123 integrate calcium imaging (C119), optogenetics (C120), ablation studies (C115, C117), and neurotransmitter identification (C118) to establish PCA's role. The compensation mechanism (C121) and insufficiency without other components (C123) are supported by the experimental data.

results.result: SPV/SPD neurons are involved in sperm initiation and possibly release, while DA-expressing socket cells play no role in initiation but are required for sperm release. Socket cells represent a non-neuronal source of DA, are proposed to be invertebrate glia, and may function hormonally as they lack DA re-uptake transporter. DA promotes the refractory period, coupling sperm release with behavioral inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C132 synthesize the roles of SPV/SPD and socket cells based on calcium imaging, ablation, and genetic data. The identification of socket cells as non-neuronal DA source (C128) is novel and well-supported. The hormonal function hypothesis (C130) is reasonable given the lack of re-uptake transporter. The coupling of DA to refractory period (C132) is experimentally demonstrated.

results.result: The authors propose that DA released during ejaculation acts to reduce post-copulatory male activity, and once DA effects are extinguished, males can mate again. The refractory period may allow circuit recovery from the large amount of signals released during copulation, which could cause receptor desensitization. Calcium transients oscillate in sex muscles following sperm movement initiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C133-C140 present mechanistic hypotheses about refractory period function. While speculative (C133-C136, C138-C139), these are reasonable interpretations of the data. The observation of oscillating Ca2+ transients (C140) and widespread cellular activation (C137) provide empirical support for the recovery hypothesis.

results.result: The authors propose that SPV and SPD regulate refractory period length by sensing sperm release. When sensory endings enter the uterus, their activity increases and sperm initiation occurs. Their activity decreases when they sense sperm release. If they don't sense intrauterine sperm, extended activity promotes continued DA release, lengthening the refractory period to allow sperm production.
results.evaluation: Claims C141-C145 present a mechanistic model for refractory period regulation based on calcium imaging data (C142-C143) and the linker cell ablation results showing variable refractory periods. While speculative (C144-C145), the model is consistent with the experimental observations.

results.result: In contrast to mammals where post-ejaculatory regulation occurs in hypothalamus, amygdala, and septal nuclei, the refractory period in C. elegans is modulated by circuitry in the male tail. However, optogenetically controlled ejaculation requires ChR2 expression in cholinergic head neurons, suggesting sexual activities are modulated by networks not directly associated with sex organs.
results.evaluation: Claims C146-C149 compare C. elegans to mammalian systems. The localization to tail circuitry (C147) is supported by the ablation and imaging data. The requirement for head neurons in optogenetic experiments (C148) supports the conclusion about distributed control (C149). The mammalian comparison (C146) is appropriately cited.

results.result: The authors draw parallels between C. elegans and mammalian ejaculatory circuits. In mammals, the dorsal nerve elicits ejaculatory responses, signals to lumbar spinothalamic (LSt) neurons in the spinal cord, which then signal neurons controlling emission and expulsion phases. C. elegans ejaculatory circuitry is similarly organized.
results.evaluation: Claims C150-C153 make comparative biology arguments. The mammalian circuit description (C150-C152) is appropriately cited. The comparison to C. elegans (C153) is supported by the circuit organization revealed in the manuscript, though the parallel is somewhat general.
